subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Verify Rolle's theorem for the function (x² − 1)(x − 2) on [−1, 2]. Find the point in the interval where the derivative vanishes.

mark_split.label: Solve f′(x) = 0 and test the roots

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.229, chapter 10 APPLICATIONS OF DERIVATIVES, the ROLLE'S AND LAGRANGE'S THEOREM sub-section, Very Short Answer question 3. MATHEMATICAL NOTE ON THE ANSWER: the stem asks for 'the point' in the singular, but f′(x) = 3x² − 4x − 1 has BOTH its roots, (2 + √7)/3 ≈ 1.549 and (2 − √7)/3 ≈ −0.215, inside (−1, 2) — checked numerically. Neither is rejected and the answer names both, since Rolle's theorem requires only one such point. recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which form of the function you use for the end values, and what you check after solving f′(x) = 0.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Check the conditions on [−1, 2]
steps.margin_note: First mark. Use the factored form for the end values and the expanded form for the derivative — each form is easier for one of the two jobs.
steps.memory_tip: A product is zero when any one bracket is zero, so the roots −1, 1 and 2 can be read straight off (x² − 1)(x − 2).
lines: f(x) = (x² − 1)(x − 2) = x³ − 2x² − x + 2, a polynomial function, so
(i) f is continuous on the closed interval [−1, 2]
(ii) f is differentiable on the open interval (−1, 2)
∴ f(−1) = f(2) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies on [−1, 2].

recall.must_convey: That f is a polynomial, continuous on [−1, 2] and differentiable on (−1, 2), and that f(−1) = f(2) = 0 because each endpoint makes one bracket zero.
accept: minus one makes the first bracket zero and two makes the second bracket zero
both end values are zero so the third condition holds

check the three conditions using the factored form

steps.why: Both ends are zeros of the product — x = −1 makes the first bracket zero and x = 2 makes the second. Reading them off the factored form is faster and safer than substituting into the expanded cubic.
common_mistakes: Expanding first and then substituting, where one sign slip in the cubic hides the fact that both end values are 0.
Writing f(−1) = (1 − 1)(−1 + 2) by getting the sign inside the second bracket wrong.

steps.label: Solve f′(x) = 0 and test the roots
steps.margin_note: Second mark. √28 = 2√7, so the 2 cancels with the 6 and the roots simplify to (2 ± √7)/3. Both pass the interval test here, so neither is rejected — but the test still has to be written.
steps.memory_tip: Simplify the surd before dividing: √28 = 2√7 turns (4 ± 2√7)/6 into (2 ± √7)/3.
lines: −1 < −0.215 < 2 and −1 < 1.549 < 2, so both roots lie in the open interval (−1, 2)

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified; the derivative vanishes at c = (2 ± √7)/3, both points lying in (−1, 2)

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = 3x² − 4x − 1 gives x = (2 ± √7)/3, and that both roots are tested and found to lie in (−1, 2).
accept: differentiate the cubic and solve the quadratic to get two plus or minus root seven over three
root twenty eight is two root seven so it simplifies to two plus or minus root seven by three
both roots are inside minus one to two so both are accepted
quadratic solve cheste two plus or minus root seven by three vasthundi
check each root lies inside the interval before writing it
heard_as: three x squared minus four x minus one

steps.why: Every root of f′ has to be tested against the open interval before it can be quoted — a root outside would have to be rejected. Here the test keeps both, and Rolle's theorem is satisfied because it requires only one such point.
common_mistakes: Differentiating the two brackets separately and multiplying the results, instead of expanding first or using the product rule.
Leaving the answer as (4 ± √28)/6 without simplifying √28 to 2√7.
Quoting a root without checking that it lies inside (−1, 2).
